content.thinking:
I'm checking the timeline discrepancy — the flag toggle by admin P1 is logged at 19:39:45, but the onset of the issue started earlier at 19:34, so the flag change can't be the actual trigger despite what C1 claims. I'm also noting that reverting the flag afterward didn't resolve things, which further undercuts the flag-toggle theory.

Both candidates collapse into the same cause, and the incident ends unresolved—likely reaches_a_cause: false, since the evidence never explains why the revert failed or why the division-by-zero occurred. The flag-toggle timestamp also contradicts the onset time, which I can't reconcile, so I'll stick to using the figure labels for timing rather than raw numbers, noting the roughly 5m46s detection delay.

Building the chain: account pages failed at a 17% average error rate (peaking near 38.5%) against a 1.5% baseline, tied to the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 that started right at onset after pages had rendered fine just before.

I'm tracing this to the monthly-spend-feature flag being evaluated on for a growing share of requests from onset, noting its state change was logged at 19:39:45 — after onset, which is a timing conflict worth flagging. Turning the flag off didn't resolve things (errors persisted for 11 more minutes), so flag-state alone doesn't explain the persistence; there were no deploys in the prior 24 hours, though three production changes appeared later in the window, and the flag provider logged one recent change. I still need to account for why the division-by-zero wasn't surfaced earlier and why errors kept going after the flag was flipped.

The actual root cause traces to a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py at line 47, but the evidence doesn't clarify what value hit zero or why disabling the flag failed to stop the errors — so this doesn't fully reach a confirmed cause. Contributing factors include no pre-enable test gating the spend summary path, an alert that only fired after a 10-minute rolling average (introducing delay), and the flag timestamp being inconsistent with the actual onset. The revert verdict also took 660 seconds, a notable delay though minor overall. I'm now drafting action items, starting with AI-1: fixing the zero-division handling in spend_summary.py.

AI-2 should focus on improving detection by alerting on per-minute error rates or a specific ZeroDivisionError log signature instead of relying solely on the 10-minute average. AI-3 is about reconciling the flag-change audit timestamp against evaluation logs, since there's a lag between the 19:39:45 P1 and evaluations starting at 19:34. AI-4 covers staging the flag rollout with an error-rate gate and automatic rollback, especially given evidence of a rapid ramp from a small subset to 100%.

Looking at what went well: Argus read all channels, reverted within seconds of the alert, and restored the flag state after refutation rather than leaving things changed. What went wrong was that the revert didn't resolve the issue, leading to 11 minutes of waiting and escalation without a confirmed root cause. There's no clear "got lucky" moment here — the error rate only peaked at 38.5%, meaning not every request failed, so I'll leave that section light.

Key assumptions to flag: the impact figures represent lower bounds, the baseline series is too short, there's a timestamp conflict on the flag toggle, and all three replicas appear to be running on the same GPU model.

I need to be careful writing the executive summary — avoid spelling out numbers like "one" or "two," avoid literal timestamps or duration figures like "11 minutes," and use placeholder labels instead so the writing stays number-free except where a digit is part of a genuine identifier like a file name. The summary should state that shopper account pages failed for a labeled duration, with error rates compared before/during/peak using placeholders, that Argus toggled the flag off without improvement, restored it, and escalated to humans with the cause still unconfirmed.

action_items.item: Reproduce the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, determine which divisor is zero, and determine why errors continued after monthly-spend-feature was switched off. Fix the division and add a test covering the zero case.
Add an alert on a short-window error rate or on the ZeroDivisionError log signature, so a sharp rise pages sooner than the 10-minute average does.
Put the monthly-spend-feature rollout behind a staged ramp that holds or rolls back automatically when the account page error rate rises.
Reconcile the flag provider's change timestamps with the evaluation logs, and record in the incident's evidence which source gives the true time the flag was enabled.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} while broken (baseline {errors_before}) and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The sustained-error alert paged at {alert_raised}, which was {alert_raised - began} after the onset.
The failing requests were logged as ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, starting at the onset. Account pages had been logged as rendering normally before it.

The spend-summary path was being reached because monthly-spend-feature evaluated on for a growing share of requests from the onset. The flag provider's change record shows the flag switched on by an admin, but that entry is stamped after the onset, so the record does not line up exactly with the log evaluations.

Switching the flag off did not help. The service stayed at the incident's level until the action was judged refuted, and the flag was then put back. So the flag state alone does not explain why the errors continued.

Nothing was deployed in the day before the incident, which rules out a code release as the trigger. The only production changes read were the flag toggles. The evidence stops here: it does not show which value is zero at spend_summary.py:47, or why the errors persisted with the flag off.

contributing_factors.factor: The sustained-error alert evaluates a 10-minute average, so paging came well after the onset ({alert_raised - began}). The flag was therefore reverted only after most of that delay had passed.
The flag went from partial to full exposure within a minute of the onset. No check was seen that gated the rollout on error rate, and no test of the spend-summary path with a zero divisor was seen.

The flag change record is stamped after the errors began, while the evaluation logs show the flag on from the onset. This made it harder to tell whether the flag was the trigger, and the revert did not resolve it.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers using io-shop saw account pages fail. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} while the service was broken, against {errors_before} beforehand, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service was still not back to normal when the incident was closed, so it was broken for at least {duration}. These figures are lower bounds. Argus found the errors came from a spend-summary feature flag that had been enabled and switched it off. The service stayed at the incident's level, so Argus judged that action refuted, put the flag back as it had been and escalated to people. The cause was not confirmed and the service was not seen recovering.

went_well: Argus read every available channel and acted on the flag candidate within seconds of the investigation starting.
Argus restored the flag to its prior state once the revert was refuted, so its own change was not left in place.
Argus escalated to people when no explanation held.
went_wrong: The leading candidate was refuted, and the service stayed at the incident's level while Argus waited for the verdict on the revert.
The incident closed with the cause unconfirmed and the service not seen recovering.
The flag change record and the logs disagree on when the flag was enabled, which weakened the trigger attribution.

input.root_cause: Account page requests failed with a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 in the spend-summary code path, which was being exercised from the onset as monthly-spend-feature evaluated on. The evidence does not show why the division fails, and it does not show why errors continued after the flag was switched off, so the underlying cause is not established.
